areas.title: School Observations
areas.subtitle: Classrooms I’ve visited
intro: I have visited more than ten preschools and kindergartens in the United States and China, and interviewed more than twenty founders, headmasters and educators.
These are notes from some of those classrooms. Schools are not named unless they have agreed to be, and no child is identified.

entries.title: A Montessori classroom in Massachusetts
entries.context: A one-hour observation for my Montessori teacher training, focused on the classroom’s layout, movement, transitions and circle time.
noticed: Each curriculum area held around six to eight materials, more in the four main areas, and each looked carefully chosen for the children’s level.
The room was spacious, without obvious runways; children spread out across the areas to work.
Every area was labelled, the hand-washing corner had small written reminders, and there was a seat set aside for a teacher to sit and observe.
practices: To go outside, a child rang a bell. Children put their work away, gathered on a line, and were called by name to fetch shoes, bags and jackets before walking out together.
Circle time began with good morning and a story, then a breathing exercise and a sharing round, passing a small stuffed animal from child to child.
The teacher used the volume of her voice to settle the room.
reflections: Transitions were still a little untidy, but the classroom stayed a relaxed environment.

entries.title: The school I attended as a child
noticed: One child built the Brown Stair into a tower almost every day, trying different ways to make it taller.
practices: When the teacher saw he had become comfortable with it, she asked if he wanted to draw his tower. As he talked about the drawing, she asked him questions and wrote them on a notecard stuck to it.

quotes.text: What I liked about this interaction was that the child’s genuine interest continued to lead the experience.
quotes.source: From a reflection written during my Montessori teacher training

quotes.text: The teacher did not decide that he had spent enough time building towers and needed to move on to something else. Instead, she observed what he was already doing and found a way to extend it.

areas.title: Montessori Experiences
areas.subtitle: Teaching and the prepared environment
areas.intro: Early childhood education is where my questions start: how to support children to reach their full potential. Montessori teacher training and time in the classroom with young children shape how I think about learning.

related.label: Peninsula Montessori Lessons, in the Workshop
Lesson Prep Planner, in the Workshop

entries.title: Teaching in a toddler classroom
body: I plan and present individual Montessori lessons for a small group of three to four children, about twelve hours a week.
Sustained observation of each child’s interests and readiness guides which activities I choose, how I adapt them, and how I document them. I also make hands-on materials and lead circle time.
With the lead teacher, I work on consistent ground rules and adult responses, and on how we support children’s growing independence.

entries.title: Assisting in a 3–6 classroom
body: A classroom of twenty children, about fifteen hours a week: individual lessons, making learning materials, and helping to observe and document children’s development.

I helped keep the prepared environment ready across several classrooms, supported independent work periods and transitions, and kept practical-care routines going, including laundry for four classrooms.
As part of my teacher training, I designed lesson plans across Practical Life, Sensorial, Math, Language and Culture.

entries.title: Becoming a Montessori teacher
body: American Montessori Society (AMS) Early Childhood teacher education, in progress.
Alongside it: the Harvard Certificate in Early Education Leadership, and training with the Massachusetts Department of Early Education and Care.

areas.title: Educational Research
areas.subtitle: Field studies, families and questions
intro: Mostly, I want to understand how children learn, and how adults can become better guides.
I’m exploring how AI can create real, positive impact, especially in education. I believe technology should strengthen meaningful human interactions rather than replace them.

entries.title: An early childhood field study, in the US and China
body: I visited more than ten preschools and kindergartens across the United States and China, and interviewed more than twenty founders, headmasters and educators about educational philosophy, child development, parents’ expectations and the challenges of early education.
In field notes and reports I compared classroom approaches, children’s independence and family expectations, and shared written observations and feedback with the educators I interviewed.

related.label: The parent-support prototypes it led to

entries.title: Reggio Emilia, Montessori’s birthplace, and Europe’s playgrounds
body: I extended the field study with visits to Reggio Emilia and to Maria Montessori’s birthplace in Italy.
Across Europe, I watched children in public play spaces, looking at learning environments, autonomy and how children play together.

related.label: Among the places in the Observatory

entries.title: A workshop for parents
body: I designed and led a two-and-a-half-hour workshop at a Montessori school in China for about ten parents, on AI, future-ready skills and activities to do at home.
Many of the parents’ questions were about educational competition, and about children falling behind.

entries.title: What I want to understand
body: How children learn, and how adults can become better guides.
Children’s independence, and how it looks different across classrooms and cultures.
What families expect from early education, and why.
How technology, including AI, can support educators and families without replacing human relationships.

areas.subtitle: The tree at the centre: still growing
areas.intro: My philosophy of education is still forming. These are sentences from my own writing, kept here as they grow.

related.label: RootMap, where these ideas meet a product

entries.title: What belongs to the adult, and what to the child

quotes.text: For me, Montessori is not about giving up control completely. It is about learning what needs to be controlled by the adult, what can belong to the child, and how the environment can create space for both the child and the teacher to learn.
quotes.source: From a reflection written during my Montessori teacher training

entries.title: Trust, and curiosity

quotes.text: The part of my practice I most want to protect is my trust in children and my curiosity about their choices.
quotes.source: From a reflection written during my Montessori teacher training

quotes.text: I want to keep being curious about why children do what they do instead of immediately deciding what they should be doing.

entries.title: When to step in, when to step back

quotes.text: I want to become better at knowing when I need to step in, when I can step back, and when something unexpected from a child is something worth following.
quotes.source: From a reflection written during my Montessori teacher training

entries.title: The teacher learns too

quotes.text: Through daily observation, thoughtful preparation, and genuine enthusiasm, the teacher learns alongside the children, guiding rather than directing, inspiring rather than instructing.
quotes.source: From my writing on the Montessori teacher

entries.title: Technology that stays human

quotes.text: I believe technology should strengthen meaningful human interactions rather than replace them.
